description: AIM, the UFW, Wounded Knee and Cesar Chavez — civil rights beyond Black-and-white America.
content_html:
Chicano Civil Rights and the United Farm Workers

The 1960s civil rights movement inspired other minority groups to demand equal treatment. Mexican Americans — often called Chicanos by activists — faced systematic discrimination in employment, education and political representation. In 1962, Cesar Chavez founded the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA) in Delano, California, alongside co-founder Dolores Huerta. Farmworkers — mostly Mexican American and Filipino — had no legal right to organise, worked in dangerous conditions for low wages and received no overtime pay.

In September 1965, the NFWA joined a Filipino farmworkers’ strike against grape growers in the Delano region, launching what became known as the Delano grape strike. Chavez used tactics consciously modelled on King’s non-violent movement: marches, fasting, and — crucially — a national consumer boycott of California grapes. By 1968, an estimated 17 million Americans were boycotting grapes. In 1970, the major grape growers signed contracts recognising the United Farm Workers (UFW). It was one of the greatest labour victories for a non-unionised workforce in US history.

Key Fact

Cesar Chavez led the Delano grape strike from 1965 to 1970, using non-violent tactics — strikes, marches, fasting and a national consumer boycott — to force grape growers to sign union recognition agreements with the UFW in 1970.

Native Americans and the American Indian Movement

Native Americans faced extreme poverty, high unemployment, poor health outcomes and broken treaty promises. In 1968, the American Indian Movement (AIM) was founded in Minneapolis by Dennis Banks and Russell Means, initially to monitor police violence against Native Americans in urban areas. AIM was influenced by Black Power and drew on a similar combination of assertive self-defence and community self-help.

In November 1969, a group of Native Americans occupied the former federal prison on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay. They held it for 19 months, drawing national attention to treaty violations and the poverty of reservation life. In November 1972, AIM participated in the “Trail of Broken Treaties,” a cross-country march to Washington DC that ended with the occupation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs building. Protesters produced a document demanding restoration of treaty-making authority and return of treaty lands.

The most dramatic confrontation came at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in February 1973. AIM members and local Oglala Lakota residents occupied the village — a site of the 1890 massacre — for 71 days, facing a federal blockade. Two Native Americans were killed during the siege; several federal agents were wounded. The FBI and federal marshals maintained the blockade. AIM leaders were subsequently prosecuted, though many charges were eventually dismissed due to government misconduct. The Church Committee later documented FBI surveillance of AIM as part of broader COINTELPRO-style operations. The occupation brought Native American land and treaty rights to national attention, though direct legislative gains were limited.

The Indian Civil Rights Act 1968

In 1968, Congress passed the Indian Civil Rights Act, which applied most Bill of Rights protections to tribal members in their dealings with tribal governments. It also recognised a degree of tribal sovereignty. The Act was a significant but limited gain: it did not restore treaty lands, and conditions on reservations remained dire. Native American activists argued that legal rights on paper were meaningless without the economic base to make them real — a critique that paralleled the Black Power movement’s dissatisfaction with the Civil Rights Act.

Beyond the UFW, the Chicano movement developed in other directions. Reies Tijerina’s Alianza Federal de Mercedes campaigned for restoration of land grants from the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Rudolfo “Corky” Gonzales founded the Crusade for Justice in Denver. Students organised walkouts (“blowouts”) in Los Angeles high schools in 1968, protesting against inadequate education for Mexican American students. These movements shared the Chicano identity label and a demand for cultural recognition alongside political rights, though they differed in tactics and focus. In 1970, La Raza Unida Party was founded to build independent Chicano political power in Texas.

Key Fact

In February–May 1973, AIM occupied Wounded Knee on the Pine Ridge Reservation for 71 days in a standoff with federal agents, protesting treaty violations and reservation conditions. Two Native Americans were killed. The occupation raised national awareness but produced limited direct legislative change.
exam_tip_html: Questions on this lesson ask about ‘civil rights campaigns for Native Americans and Chicanos.’ Cover both groups, not just one. For each group, give specific examples: UFW and Delano (Chicano), AIM and Wounded Knee (Native American). Show you can make connections — both groups were influenced by the Black civil rights movement, both used a mix of legal action, direct action and cultural assertion. The Indian Civil Rights Act 1968 is the key piece of federal legislation to cite for Native Americans. Examiners reward students who identify the limits of legislative gains as well as the achievements.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta led the UFW to victory in the Delano grape strike (1965–1970) using non-violent tactics including a national consumer boycott, winning union recognition for farmworkers.
  • AIM, founded in 1968, organised the Alcatraz occupation (1969–71), the Trail of Broken Treaties (1972) and the Wounded Knee standoff (1973) to demand restoration of treaty rights and highlight reservation poverty.
  • Both movements gained public attention and some legal recognition, but both argued that paper rights without economic restoration were insufficient — an echo of Black Power’s critique of civil rights legislation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Delano grape strike led by Cesar Chavez.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the strike and gives specific detail, e.g. Chavez organised a national consumer boycott of California grapes; by 1968 an estimated 17 million Americans were boycotting grapes, forcing growers to negotiate. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to a farmworkers' strike. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the American Indian Movement (AIM) in the years 1968 to 1973.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) AIM was founded in Minneapolis in 1968 to monitor police violence against Native Americans in urban areas, influenced by Black Power; (2) in 1973 AIM members occupied Wounded Knee for 71 days in a standoff with federal agents, protesting treaty violations and reservation conditions. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Chicano civil rights movement drew on similar tactics to the African American civil rights movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — Chavez consciously modelled his approach on King's non-violent direct action (marches, fasting, boycotts); the Brown v Board precedent showed courts could be used; the Civil Rights Act opened possibilities for Title VII employment claims; both movements faced similar structural discrimination. Shows the connection between the movements. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes the tactics without explaining the connection. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Wounded Knee occupation of 1973 was significant for Native American civil rights.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) the 71-day occupation brought national media attention to treaty violations and reservation poverty that had been largely ignored; (2) it demonstrated AIM's ability to organise a sustained confrontation with federal authorities, showing the scale of Native American grievance and building movement solidarity. Secure: Two reasons with evidence. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant were the campaigns of Cesar Chavez and the UFW in improving the lives of Chicano Americans?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis covering gains (union recognition for farmworkers in 1970; national consumer boycott demonstrated Latino political power; inspired wider Chicano movement) and limits (farmworkers remained among the poorest workers; UFW membership later declined; broader housing and educational inequality unchanged). Compares UFW's significance to other parts of the Chicano movement and to Native American campaigns. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Chavez without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the impact of civil rights campaigns for Native Americans and Chicanos in the years 1962 to 1974.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering both groups — UFW, grape boycott, union victory (Chicano); AIM, Alcatraz, Trail of Broken Treaties, Wounded Knee, Indian Civil Rights Act (Native American). Reaches an integrated judgement about what changed and what remained limited, comparing the two movements. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events with limited structure or covers only one group. Emerging: Brief narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: What did Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta found in 1962?
options: The National Farm Workers Association (later UFW)

knowledge_checks.q: How long did the AIM occupation of Wounded Knee last in 1973?
The Delano _____ strike began in 1965 and ended in union victory for farmworkers in 1970.
The American Indian Movement (AIM) was founded in _____ in 1968 by Dennis Banks and Russell Means.
Match each event to its civil rights group:

flashcard_questions.q: When did Cesar Chavez found the NFWA?
flashcard_questions.a: 1962, in Delano, California, with co-founder Dolores Huerta.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Delano grape strike begin and when did it end in victory?
flashcard_questions.a: September 1965; grape growers signed UFW contracts in 1970.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the key tactic Chavez added to the farmworker strike?
flashcard_questions.a: A national consumer boycott of California grapes, with 17 million Americans participating by 1968.

flashcard_questions.q: When was AIM founded and by whom?
flashcard_questions.a: 1968, in Minneapolis, by Dennis Banks and Russell Means.
Native Americans occupied the former federal prison for 19 months to draw attention to treaty violations.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Trail of Broken Treaties?
flashcard_questions.a: A 1972 cross-country march to Washington DC by AIM, ending in occupation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs building.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Indian Civil Rights Act 1968?
flashcard_questions.a: It applied most Bill of Rights protections to tribal members and recognised a degree of tribal sovereignty.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the term 'Chicano' refer to?
flashcard_questions.a: A term used by Mexican American activists from the late 1960s to emphasise cultural pride and political self-determination.

glossary_terms.definition: A term used by Mexican American activists from the late 1960s to describe themselves, emphasising cultural pride and political self-determination.

Labour organiser and civil rights leader who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association (later UFW) in 1962 and used non-violent tactics including strikes and boycotts to win rights for farmworkers.
A five-year strike and consumer boycott (1965–1970) led by Chavez and the UFW against grape growers in California, which won union recognition for farmworkers.
A Native American civil rights organisation founded in Minneapolis in 1968 that combined urban Native activism with treaty rights campaigning.
A 71-day armed standoff in February–May 1973 at the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, where AIM members occupied the village to protest tribal governance and broken treaties.
